Once something has reached a person, pressure and persuasion change how hard the response is without changing whose response it is. That is a demanding position, and the Quran does not soften it by giving either side the last word: the argument simply continues into the next ayah and then stops.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answer to this reply, naming scheming by night and day as the pressure applied.
Has the proud concede the point differently, saying guidance came and they all went astray.
Stages the same exchange with the reply that they had no authority over anyone.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this reply is a question, and that questions are how people push responsibility back without saying anything false. Listen for one this week, in a meeting or at home, and notice how effective it is. Then notice whether you use the same move yourself. Most of us do, and it is nearly invisible from the inside.

studies.title: They Will Hide Their Remorse
studies.meaning: The last turn in the exchange names the pressure precisely: scheming by night and day, and an instruction to reject God and set up rivals. Then the argument simply stops, and the ayah describes something nobody says aloud. They conceal their remorse when they see what is coming. The commentators read the concealment as the point of the whole scene. Regret has arrived in both parties at once and neither will show it, so the dispute ends without a verdict from either side.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a three-part exchange between those who led and those who followed. The commentators treat the scene as belonging to the Day of Resurrection and note the Quran's habit of ending such disputes without awarding the argument. The description of scheming through the night and the day is read as the sustained, ordinary pressure of a society rather than any single conspiracy.

keyTerms.note: A word for working on something indirectly, by arrangement rather than by force. Attached here to night and day, it describes pressure applied continuously and by ordinary means rather than a plot with a moment.
A plural for peers or matches, things placed on a level with something else. The word names the relation claimed rather than the object, so what is denied is a status rather than an existence.

A verb for keeping something inside, from the root behind the word for a secret. Used of remorse it describes a feeling present and withheld, which is the last thing the scene reports about either group.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Showing regret in public was costly in a society organised by standing. A man who admitted he had been wrong in front of an assembly gave up something he could not easily get back, and the habit of not conceding was learned young and practised daily. What the ayah describes at the end is a room full of people all feeling the same thing and all declining, out of long habit, to be the first to say it.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase for concealing remorse occurs twice in the Quran, here and in a passage describing what those who wronged would give to ransom themselves. In both places it is the last thing said about the people involved, after the arguing has finished. The classical commentators note the placement in both cases.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Remorse appears in the scene and changes nothing, which is a claim about what repentance actually requires. Feeling it is evidently not sufficient, since these people feel it fully. What is missing is the acknowledgement, and the ayah shows the habit of withholding that surviving even here. Repentance in the Quran's account is therefore an act rather than a state, and the difference is exactly what this scene is built to show.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for concealed remorse, after describing what they would give to ransom themselves.
Opens the exchange this ayah closes, with the accusation the leaders were answering.
Records the same acknowledgement finally spoken aloud, and the answer that it receives.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you were sorry and did not say so, because saying it would have cost more than staying quiet. Nearly everyone has one. This ayah describes exactly that habit persisting at the very last moment. Pick the smallest current instance and say the sentence out loud this week to the person concerned.

studies.title: Its Affluent Always Said No
studies.meaning: A pattern is stated without exception: no warner was ever sent to a town whose comfortable class did not reject him. The second ayah quotes their reasoning, and it is an argument from evidence as they see it. We have more wealth and more children, so we will not be punished. The reply does not dispute the wealth. It relocates it, saying provision is spread out or restricted by God's will, which severs the link between having and standing well.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a city whose leading families were also its wealthiest. The commentators note that the pattern described here matches the accounts of earlier communities given elsewhere in the Quran, where opposition consistently comes from those with the most to lose. No particular occasion is reported, and the passage reads as a generalisation the audience could check against stories they already knew.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from a verb meaning to be given a life of luxury, so the word describes people to whom comfort was done rather than people who achieved it. It occurs five times in the Quran, always of opposition.
A verb for laying something flat and wide, used of a garment or a hand opened. It pictures provision as a surface being extended rather than as an amount being counted out.
From the root for determining an amount. It is not a word for withholding, so the pair describes two ways of apportioning rather than generosity set against meanness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was visibly connected to divine favour in the ordinary understanding of the place. The families who ran the sanctuary were the families who ran the caravans, and the prosperity of both was taken as evidence that the arrangement was working. Numbers of sons were counted the same way, since a man with many was protected in disputes. The argument quoted here was simply how the city read its own success.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those living in ease occurs five times in the Quran, and in every one of them the people it names are the ones resisting a message or facing its consequence. The classical commentators treat that consistency as significant, since the term itself carries no moral charge; what is repeated is the situation, not the word's meaning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer given does not condemn wealth or deny that it comes from God. It denies that its distribution carries information about anyone's standing. That is a sharper move than a warning against riches, because it leaves the comfortable with their comfort and takes away only the inference they were drawing from it. The closing clause, that most people do not know, applies to the reasoning rather than to the fact.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same pattern, with those living in ease saying they found their fathers on a way.
Names the same class among an earlier people as the ones who denied the meeting to come.
Corrects the same inference directly, that honour and restriction are verdicts on a person.

studies.applyIt: Notice how quickly you read someone's circumstances as a verdict on them, in either direction. The colleague doing well, the friend whose year has gone badly. This passage removes exactly that inference without saying anything about the circumstances themselves. Catch yourself making it once this week and simply drop the conclusion, keeping the observation.

studies.title: What Brings You Near
studies.meaning: The claim of the previous ayat is answered by naming what does not do the work. Neither wealth nor children bring anyone close, and then an exception follows that changes the subject of the sentence: it is the one who believes and acts well. The commentators note the grammar, since the exception replaces a possession with a person. What follows is a reward described as doubled and a place named by a word for upper rooms, with security attached to it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the exchange about the affluent and their inference from prosperity. The surah has denied that wealth indicates favour; this ayah supplies what does. Commentators read the mention of upper rooms as answering the same audience in its own terms, since the tallest and best-appointed houses in a town belonged to precisely the families whose reasoning has just been dismantled.

keyTerms.note: A noun for closeness of position, from a root also used of drawing something forward. It names a place in relation to someone rather than an emotion, which is why possessions could plausibly have been thought to secure it.
The definite form of the word for a multiple, so a doubling already known rather than newly announced. The Quran uses the same term elsewhere for a reward increased beyond what a deed would earn.
A plural for rooms built above the ground floor. This exact plural occurs only here in the Quran, and the word describes the most desirable part of a house in a hot country.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An upper room was a mark of standing in an Arabian town. It caught what breeze there was, sat above the dust and the animals, and was where a household received people it wished to honour. Only substantial houses had one. Promising upper chambers to those who believe and act well takes the exact architectural sign of wealth and reassigns it on a different basis entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: The plural word for upper chambers used in this ayah occurs only here in the Quran, though a related form appears elsewhere for the same promise. The Quran's descriptions of the hereafter frequently borrow the vocabulary of the best available things in that society, gardens, running water, and here the upper storey of a good house.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception in the middle of the ayah does more than correct a mistake. By replacing possessions with a person as the thing that draws near, it changes what kind of thing nearness is. Wealth and children are held; belief and good action are done. And the security named at the end answers the anxiety that actually drives accumulation, so what is promised is precisely what the wealth in the previous ayat was being used to buy.

crossReferences.why: States the claim this ayah answers, that more wealth and children mean no punishment.
Promises the same upper chambers with rivers beneath them, to those who work well.
Lists wealth and children among the loves made attractive to people, then names what is better.

studies.applyIt: Ask what your savings are actually for. Under the practical answers there is usually one word, and it is security. This ayah names that word directly and attaches it to something else. You do not have to change your finances today. Just notice, once, what you have been asking money to do that it was never able to do.

studies.title: Whatever You Spend Is Replaced
studies.meaning: This answers something quoted a few ayat earlier, where people point at their wealth and their sons as proof that nothing will befall them. Provision is described as spread wide or drawn close by a decision, and the decision is explicitly not a verdict on the person. Then a promise: whatever you spend is replaced. The verb is the one used of a successor stepping into the place of the one before, so what is described is substitution rather than repayment, and the currency of the replacement is left unstated.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The preceding ayat quote objectors saying that they have more wealth and more children and will therefore not be punished, and the reply denies that either brings anyone closer. The community hearing this had watched members lose trade and standing for accepting the message, so whether prosperity indicated approval was not a philosophical question for them but a daily one.

keyTerms.note: The verb for unrolling a cloth or opening a hand flat. Provision is pictured as something laid out to a width rather than counted, which is why its opposite in the same sentence is measuring.
From the root of measure and capacity, not of withholding. Restriction is described as an exact allotment rather than a refusal, which removes the sense of a punishment being administered.
From the root that gives the word for a successor. What is promised is something taking the place of what was spent, which is a different claim from the same thing being returned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was visible and it moved fast. A merchant's capital travelled with a caravan for months, and a household cut out of the trading network by its neighbours lost everything measurable within a season. Giving away goods in that setting was not an abstraction about generosity: it was removing part of the stock that a family's survival through the next year depended on.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for replacing in this ayah comes from the same root as the word used for a successor placed on the earth, and the word for someone who comes after another and takes their position. The promise is therefore worded not as a refund but as a succession: something else steps into the vacancy that the spending made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas that people habitually fuse are separated in consecutive sentences: that provision is distributed by God, which is affirmed, and that its size measures His approval, which is denied. The promise about spending then reverses the arithmetic everyone assumes, that giving is subtraction. Leaving the form of the replacement unstated is deliberate, since naming it would turn the promise into an investment scheme.

crossReferences.why: Names the two voices in the decision: one promising poverty, the other promising forgiveness and bounty.
Puts the same movement as a loan offered to God and multiplied many times over on return.
Shows the regret of someone asking for a short delay in order to give, when the time has run out.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week at a moment when it is mildly inconvenient rather than comfortable: before payday rather than after, from what you were saving rather than from what was left over. Then watch what actually happens over the following month, without arranging anything to make the ayah come true.
